canonical_text:
Contemporary Bermuda is a self-governing British Overseas Territory whose
economy, society, and institutions are shaped by two persistent forces:
its geography (an isolated mid-Atlantic island chain with no arable scale
and a reef shelter that produced the early salvage and salt economies)
and its history (slavery, the 1834 emancipation, and the 1968
constitutional settlement that put a Black-majority population in
political control of an internationally-exposed financial centre).

canonical_text: Bermuda's mid-Atlantic position, lack of arable land, reef shelter, and tropical climate together explain the economic structure of the islands — from the seventeenth-century salt trade through tourism to today's reinsurance sector.

The 1968 Constitution Order is the founding instrument of contemporary self-government; the political settlement that produced it traces back through the 1834 emancipation, the slavery period, and the colonial era.

Bermuda's demographic structure — Black majority since the nineteenth century, Portuguese-Bermudian minority, declining fertility — produced the cultural institutions (AME church, Cup Match, Gombey troupes) that define contemporary Bermudian life.

The same geography that produced the economy also produces the cost structure: import-everything supply chains, expensive housing, and utilities pricing that explain why a single resident's monthly outlay exceeds OECD medians by roughly three times.

The Bermudian-status / Permanent Resident Certificate / work-permit framework determines who may live and work on the islands, and that framework is shaped by the same labour-market pressures the rest of the book traces.

The education, healthcare, and transportation institutions — Bermuda College, KEMH, MWI, the ferry/scooter mobility regime — are the lived-experience surface of the deeper economic and constitutional structures.

Bermuda has nine traditional parishes including St. George's. Any chapter
that names a different count contradicts the manual's canonical fact.

The Bermudian dollar is pegged at parity with the US dollar. Any chapter
that implies otherwise contradicts the manual.

L. F. Wade International Airport sits on St. David's Island in St.
George's Parish. Any chapter that places it elsewhere contradicts the
canonical-facts document.
